newsitem.title: UK: Strong pound hits UK export orders -- CBI survey.
newsitem.headline: Strong pound hits UK export orders -- CBI survey.

text.p: Demand for British manufactured exports has levelled off for the first time since October 1993, according to the latest quarterly industrial trends survey of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI).
Manufacturing output grew steadily over the past four months although more slowly than expected. The CBI said a decision on whether British interest rates needed to rise or not was finely balanced.
Twenty-three percent of firms reported higher export orders over the past four months and 24 percent reported lower orders, a negative balance of one percent.
"The impact of sterling's strength is beginning to feed through to manufacturers' export orders," said Ross Buckland, a member of the CBI's economic affairs committee.

"Companies are becoming concerned about the export outlook and this is reflected by the fall in optimism about export prospects and the rise in the proportion of companies reporting that prices are a constraint on their ability to win export orders." Optimism about export prospects for the year ahead fell for the first time since October 1993, with a negative balance of two percent more firms reporting optimism had fallen than risen.
Over the coming four months firms expect the growth in export orders to pick up, but the CBI noted that demand expectations had not been fully met since APril 1995.
Buckland said domestic demand for UK-produced consumer goods in particular continued to improve, although the pace of growth was now slower than at the end of last year.
"With the output recovery expected to continue, but manufacturing cost and prices pressures encouragingly weak, the decision about raising interest rates is finely balanced."
The survey showed firms expected growth in manufacturing output to be more robust over the next four months.
But their expectations were less positive for the second consecutive survey.
It noted that expectations had not been fully met in any of the last seven quarterly surveys.
Manufacturers reported that total orders had slowed over the last four months instead of picking up as expected.
Overall 32 percent of firms reported higher orders and 24 percent lower, giving a positive balance of eight percent reporting higher demand over the past four months.
Domestic orders rose very slightly, with a positive balance of one percent of firms saying orders were higher.
"Firms expect domestic orders to rise strongly over the coming four months, with a balance of 16 percent more firms expecting orders to rise than to fall.
The CBI said the prospects for output price inflation were fairly promising, with unit costs levelling off and expected to remain flat over the next four months.

Domestic prices fell for the third consecutive survey, contrary to expectations. "They are expected to pick up over the coming four months but are below those expected at this time last year and reflect firms revising list prices at the beginning of the year," the CBI said.
"Export prices fell steadily and for the third consecutive survey and are expected to remain unchanged over the coming four months."
Business confidence increased for the third consecutive survey and at about the same rate as in October.
Manufacturers reported a slight rise in stocks of work in progress while stocks of raw materials and finished stocks fell slightly, although not by as much as had been expected.
Firms reported a sharped fall in manufacturing jobs over the past four months, with a similar rate of fall expected over the coming months.
Manufacturers continued to report firm positive plans to invest in plant and machinery over the coming yuear, although intentions were less buoyant than those recorded last October.
Plans to increase spending on training and ininovation remained strong. The percentage of firms working below capacity rose slightly to 52 percent following a slight fall in the last survey.
The CBI said 1,033 manufacturers, representing 50 industries and accounting for around half of Britain's manufacturing employment and exports, took part in its survey.
It was conducted between December 13 anad January 8.
-- Richard Murphy, London Newsroom 44 171 542 2774
